FrontPanelPortGroup.description:
A list of front-panel ports to represent multiple ports with a single port_name. This allows connection types to accept a set of ports instead of a single port, but not all connection types accept groups.
The ingress distribution setting specifies how the configuration is to be distributed to the ports. The configuration (e.g. the vlans to route) can be either copied or split equally amongst the ingress ports. Split is the default, as would typically be the case for non-lag port groups, where traffic is unique on each port. Copy is typically used for lag port groups, where traffic might be sent to any port.
Egress distribution is always split. All egress ports must have link up to avoid a loss of traffic (assuming ingress traffic is uniformly distributed).

ConnectVlanVxlan.description:
Reencapsulates VLan traffic to VxLAN traffic between two endpoints. This can be useful when connecting equipment that supports VLAN but not VxLAN to equipment that requires VxLAN.
One of the endpoints must be tagged "vlan", and the other "vxlan". Traffic arriving on the vlan-tagged endpoint is reencapsulated and sent to the  vxlan-tagged endpoint using the VLAN ID of the traffic to determine the  VNI of the untagged endpoint. Likewise, traffic from the vxlan-tagged endpoint is reencapsulated as VLAN traffic with the VLAN ID for the vlan-tagged endpoint being derived from the VNI of the VxLAN traffic from the vxlan-tagged  endpoint.
If the traffic received on a vxlan-tagged endpoint arrives on a VLAN (of the outermost Ethernet), the VLAN will be discarded. And the traffic will appear on the VLAN of the vlan-tagged endpoint. If the inner, VxLAN-enclosed, packet is on a VLAN, then that. will become the inner VLAN of the traffic exiting the vlan-tagged endpoint.
If the traffic arriving on the vlan-tagged endpoint is Q-in-Q, then the inner VLAN ID becomes the outer VLAN of the VxLAN-encapsulated packet leaving the vxlan-tagged port.
The vxlan_settings that are configured as ranges need only specify the start value, in which case the count will be the vlan count of the vlan-tagged endpoint.

ConnectVlanNvgre.description:
Reencapsulates VLan traffic to NVGRE traffic between two endpoints. This can be useful when connecting equipment that supports VLAN but not NVGRE to equipment that requires NVGRE.
One of the endpoints must be tagged "vlan", and the other "nvgre". Traffic arriving on the vlan-tagged endpoint is reencapsulated and sent to the  NVGRE-tagged endpoint using the VLAN ID of the traffic to determine the  VSID of the untagged endpoint. Likewise, traffic from the nvgre-tagged endpoint is reencapsulated as VLAN traffic with the VLAN ID for the vlan-tagged endpoint being derived from the VSID of the NVGRE traffic from the NVGRE-tagged  endpoint.
If the traffic received on a NVGRE-tagged endpoint arrives on a VLAN (of the outermost Ethernet), the VLAN will be discarded. And the traffic will appear  on the VLAN of the vlan-tagged endpoint. If the inner, NVGRE-enclosed, packet is on a VLAN, then that will become the inner VLAN of the traffic exiting the  vlan-tagged endpoint.
If the traffic arriving on the vlan-tagged endpoint is Q-in-Q, then the inner VLAN ID becomes the outer VLAN of the NVGRE-encapsulated packet leaving the nvgre-tagged port.
The nvgre_settings that are configured as ranges need only specify the start value, in which case the count will be the vlan count of the vlan-tagged endpoint.

Connection.description:
A two-or-more-way connection between Ethernet ports that optionally transforms the data (i.e. a "bump in the wire").
Multiple connections can connect to any given port, but the transforms for source ports should be uniquely specified to avoid undefined behavior. For example, a single source port might use two ARP  connections going to two different destination ports. In that case one connection could route VLAN ARPs and the other could route non_VLAN ARPs (or a different range of ARPs) so that each  would carries unique traffic.
All connection types can perform encap/decap of VLAN traffic bidirectionally. Some connection types can perform encap/decap to/from other protocols as well. The term tunnel ID in the following descriptions is used to describe either VLAN IDs or the tunnel identifiers of other protocols (e.g. VNIs for VxLAN).
Traffic arriving on an endpoint with a tunnel IDs outside of the ID or range specified in an endpoint's configuration are ignored. Additional connections may be added with non-overlapping sets of tunnel IDs to route and/or process different sets differently.
When an endpoint is specified with a single tunnel ID, and a packet arrives at that endpoint with a matching ID, then the packet is routed to the opposite endpoint(s) and receives the tunnel ID (or first ID of a range) of the opposite endpoint.
When an endpoint is specified with a range of tunnel IDs, and a packet arrives that endpoint with a matching ID, then the offset from the start of that endpoint's range. The packet is  routed to the opposite endpoint(s) and receives the tunnel ID from the opposite endpoint's  tunnel ID or range. If the opposite endpoint is a single ID, then, of course, that is the outgoing tunnel ID. If it is a range, however, then the offset from the incoming endpoint is added to the start of the outgoing endpoint's range. If only one of the endpoints has a count, then that count is used for both. If two endpoints have a different count, however, then the outgoing tunnel ID is according to the following equation:
tunnel_id_out = tunnel_id_in + ( input_offset modulo range_count_out )
So if the incoming range is less than the outgoing range count, then the result is the same as if the counts were the same. But if the it is the outgoing range count is smaller, then the incoming ranges are wrapped around.
